slides.headline: A lion. A sleeping woman. Then what?
Paris, 1897
slides.text: A painter who never left France paints a desert under a full moon. A woman sleeps in the sand. But she is not alone.

slides.headline: The visitor
slides.text: A lion pads up behind her, tail raised, and lowers its head to sniff her. Any second now, surely. But it doesn't strike.

slides.headline: Fast asleep
slides.text: She sleeps on, in a striped robe, staff in hand. The painter's own words: the lion picks up her scent "yet does not devour her."

slides.headline: Her only things
slides.text: Beside her lie a mandolin and a water jar. He called her a wandering mandolin player. Now look at the sand around her.

slides.headline: No footprints
slides.text: No footprints anywhere. No trail, no path. How did she, or the lion, get here? Some see the whole scene as a dream.

slides.headline: Who dreamed it?
slides.text: And the dreamer? Henri Rousseau, a self-taught painter who worked at the Paris toll gates. Friends nicknamed him Le Douanier, the customs officer.

slides.headline: His hometown said no
slides.text: In 1898 he offered it to Laval, the town where he was born. Laval turned it down. Then the painting simply disappeared.

slides.headline: Found in 1924
slides.text: It resurfaced in 1924, at a Paris charcoal merchant's, and later reached MoMA. So tell us: what does the lion do next?
